title: Quick-Fire Review: Questions and Glossary
subtitle: The question bank, answer skeletons, Top 60 and the A to Z

scenes.title: Quick-Fire Review: Questions and Glossary
scenes.subtitle: The question bank, answer skeletons, Top 60 and the A to Z

steps.say: Welcome to the System Design Workshop, episode thirty-two, the last one: Quick-Fire Review, Questions and Glossary. A fast lap around everything, the way interviewers ask it.
By the end you'll give a one-line skeleton for the most-asked Design X prompts, answer concept questions in thirty seconds, and define key terms from A to Z.
It follows Module twenty-two, the question bank, plus the Top sixty and the glossary at the end of Module zero. Treat it as a drill: pause, answer out loud, then compare.

scenes.title: How to use the question bank
bullets: ★ = asked again and again: drill those first
Part A: 'Design X' prompts, each as a short outline
Part B: concept questions with 30-second answers
Drill: read, cover, answer aloud, then compare
Mark what you stumbled on; redo it the next day
Part A timing: 2-minute outline, then one deep dive
scenes.caption: Book: Module 22 · How to use this bank

steps.say: First, how to use the bank. A star marks a question asked again and again. Do those first.
Part A is the Design X prompts, each an outline in whiteboard order: requirements, components, probes, then scale.
Part B is concept questions, each answered in about thirty seconds.
The drill is simple. Read the question, cover the answer, say yours out loud or sketch the boxes, then compare.
Mark the ones you stumbled on, and redo them the next day.
For Part A, time yourself. Two minutes for the outline, then pick one deep dive and go further.

scenes.title: Drilling one prompt: the URL shortener
bullets: Read: 'Design TinyURL.' Cover the outline, start 2 minutes
Requirements: 7-char codes, reads 100 to 1 over writes
Components: key generator, KV store, Redis, CDN
Probes: base62 counter, 301 vs 302, duplicate URLs
Compare: forgot 302 for analytics? Mark it, redo tomorrow

steps.say: Let's run the drill once. Read: design TinyURL. Cover the answer and start a two-minute timer.
Requirements: seven-character codes, fast redirects, reads outnumber writes a hundred to one.
Components: a key generator, a key-value store, a Redis cache, and redirects behind a C-D-N.
Probes: how you make the key, three-oh-one versus three-oh-two, and what happens when the same long U-R-L arrives twice.
Now compare. Forgot that analytics needs a three-oh-two? Mark it, and redo it tomorrow.

head: Prompt
One-line answer skeleton
rows: base62 counter key, KV store, cache, CDN
token bucket in gateway, atomic Redis, 429
hash ring, N=3, R+W>N, LSM, gossip
frontier per host, Bloom filter, politeness

steps.say: Now Part A, by category. First, building blocks. URL shortener: base-sixty-two encode a counter, store it in a key-value store, cache it, redirect behind a C-D-N.
Rate limiter: a token bucket in the gateway, an atomic check-and-increment in Redis, and a four-twenty-nine with Retry-After.
Unique I-D generator: a Snowflake I-D. Forty-one bits of milliseconds, ten bits of worker I-D, twelve bits of sequence. No coordination needed.
Key-value store: a consistent-hash ring, three replicas, quorums where R plus W is greater than N, an L-S-M storage engine, and gossip for membership.
Web crawler: one frontier queue per host for politeness, and a Bloom filter for U-R-Ls already seen.
Message queue: brokers holding partitioned append-only logs, in-sync replicas for durability, and consumers that track offsets. The bank also covers caches, notifications, locks, login and webhooks.
Worked number: seven characters from sixty-two symbols gives about three and a half trillion codes. At a thousand new links a second, that lasts a hundred years.
And the redirect choice: a three-oh-one is permanent, so browsers cache it and your load drops. A three-oh-two sends every click back to you, which you need for analytics. Say which you want and why.

head: Prompt
One-line answer skeleton
rows: hybrid fan-out: push normal, pull celebrities
timeline cache per user, Snowflake IDs sort it
pre-signed upload to object store, CDN reads
inverted index, shard by doc, scatter-gather
Redis sorted set per user, trim to last 20

steps.say: Second, social and content. News feed: push post I-Ds to followers for normal users, pull celebrities' posts at read time.
Twitter: per-user timeline caches in Redis lists, and Snowflake I-Ds give time order for free.
Instagram: clients upload straight to object storage with a pre-signed U-R-L, and the C-D-N serves most reads.
TikTok: retrieve by embedding, rank about a thousand, re-rank, and preload the next videos.
Search engine: an inverted index sharded by document, queried by scatter-gather.
Recently viewed: one Redis sorted set per user, scored by timestamp, trimmed to the last twenty.

scenes.title: Hybrid fan-out
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  P["New post"] --> F{"Millions of followers?"}
  F -->|"no"| W["Push ID into follower feeds"]
  F -->|"yes"| S["Store once, no fan-out"]
  W --> R["Read feed"]
  S -->|"merge at read"| R
scenes.caption: Push for most users, pull for the few huge accounts

steps.say: Imagine fifty million followers. Fan-out on write means fifty million cache writes per post. Fan-out on read makes every read slow.

So split it. A normal user's post is pushed into each follower's cache. A celebrity's post is stored once, and merged in when a follower reads their feed. Reads stay fast, and no single post causes a write storm.

scenes.title: Design X: counting, ranking, analytics

head: Prompt
One-line answer skeleton
rows: growth versus baseline, not raw volume
N sub-counters per hot item, sum on read
heartbeats into an expiring set per page
Kafka, stream rollups, columnar OLAP, HLL

scenes.caption: Book: Module 22 · Counting, ranking and analytics

steps.say: Third, counting, ranking and analytics. Top K: per-minute counts, and a count-min sketch plus a heap when exact counts cost too much.
Trending means growth, not volume, so good morning doesn't trend every day.
Like counter: a viral post makes one counter row hot, so split it into sub-counters and sum on read.
N users viewing this page: clients heartbeat every ten to thirty seconds into a per-page set with expiry, and you count the fresh entries.
Ad clicks: billing needs exactly-once effect, so checkpoints, idempotent sinks, and watermarks for late events.
Analytics: Kafka, stream rollups, and a columnar O-L-A-P store.

scenes.title: Top K over the last hour
bullets: Keep 60 one-minute buckets of counts per item
Each minute: drop the oldest bucket, add the newest
Each partition computes a local top K
Merge: take more than K per partition, e.g. 2K
Fast approximate stream path, exact nightly batch

steps.say: Top K for the last hour, over millions of shares a second. Step one: keep sixty one-minute buckets of counts.
Step two: every minute, drop the oldest bucket and add the newest. The hourly count is the sum of sixty numbers.
Step three: events are partitioned by article, so each partition computes its own top K.
Step four: merge the partial lists. Take somewhat more than K from each partition, say twice K, so an item that's tenth everywhere isn't lost.
Step five: serve the fast approximate answer now; a batch job gives exact numbers later.

head: Prompt
One-line answer skeleton
rows: shard by user, SPF, DKIM, DMARC
pub/sub per stream, gateways fan out, sample
Redis sorted set: ZINCRBY, rank, top N
one server owns a table, append move log

steps.say: Fourth, messaging and real-time. Chat: WebSocket gateways, a registry of who's on which gateway, and a server-assigned sequence number per conversation.
Email: shard by user, and authenticate senders with S-P-F, D-K-I-M and D-MARC, so your mail lands in inboxes, not spam.
Live comments: one pub-sub topic per stream, and gateways subscribe, so one message per gateway crosses the network, not one per viewer.
Zoom: media over U-D-P, because a late packet is useless, and a selective forwarding unit that forwards streams without decoding.
Leaderboard: a Redis sorted set. Update the score, get my rank, get the top ten, each in log time.
Card game: one server owns each table and is the only one that changes it, with an append-only move log for crash recovery.

scenes.title: Live comments on a huge stream
scenes.caption: impossible and unreadable, so fan out twice and sample

steps.say: Imagine one stream with a million viewers posting five thousand comments a second. Sending every comment to every viewer is five billion deliveries a second. Impossible, and nobody could read it.
So fan out in two levels: comment service, pub-sub, a few thousand gateways, then local sockets. And above a threshold, send each viewer a sample, friends first, at a readable rate like ten a second.

head: Prompt
One-line answer skeleton
rows: in-memory geo index, match by ETA, no double-assign
geohash prefix plus 8 neighbours, or quadtree
pub/sub channel per user, TTL on location
dispatch to food-ready time, batch orders

steps.say: Fifth, location. Uber: driver locations in an in-memory geo index. Match by arrival time, and use a conditional update so a driver is never assigned twice.
Yelp: a geohash prefix search plus the eight neighbouring cells, or a quadtree that adapts to density.
Nearby friends: a channel per user, friends subscribe and filter by distance.
Google Maps: tiles on a C-D-N, and precomputed routing hierarchies for fast routes.
Food delivery: dispatch the courier for when the food will be ready, not when it was ordered, and batch two or three orders per courier.
Surge pricing: demand over supply per hexagon cell, smoothed, with the quoted price locked for a few minutes.

scenes.title: Food delivery by the numbers
bullets: 3M orders a day, about 125 a second at dinner peak
300K couriers send GPS every 5 seconds
300,000 ÷ 5 = 60,000 location writes a second
So: locations in memory, history written async
Orders: a saga with timers; pickup is no return

steps.say: Let's put numbers on food delivery. Three million orders a day is about a hundred and twenty-five a second at the dinner peak. That's modest.
But three hundred thousand couriers each send a G-P-S point every five seconds.
Three hundred thousand divided by five is sixty thousand location writes a second. That's the heaviest load in the system, far above orders.
So the design follows: keep live locations in memory, sharded by zone, and write history asynchronously.
The order itself is a saga, with durable timers for a restaurant that goes silent. Once the courier picks up, there's no going back.

scenes.title: Two-stream plan. A phone dies mid-movie. Counter or lease?
bullets: A counter: +1 on start, -1 on stop
A lease per stream with a TTL, renewed by heartbeats

steps.say: Pause and think. A Netflix plan allows two streams. A phone dies mid-movie and never sends stop. Do you track this with a counter or with leases? Answer next.

head: Prompt
One-line answer skeleton
rows: parallel chunk transcode, adaptive bitrate, CDN
push catalog to ISP caches overnight
ingest, live transcode, short HLS segments
prefetch next track; exact royalty counts
5 to 8 MB parts, ask which parts arrived

steps.say: The answer is leases, and that's our sixth category, media. YouTube: transcode chunks in parallel into many bitrates, and let the player pick each segment's quality from its bandwidth.
Netflix: the catalog is known ahead of time, so push content to its own caches inside internet providers overnight, instead of pulling on demand.
Screen limit: a lease per stream with a time to live. A counter leaks when a device dies without saying stop. A lease just expires.
Twitch: live transcode into short H-L-S segments; shorter cuts delay but adds load.
Spotify: prefetch the next track, and keep royalty counts exact.
Resumable upload: chunks of five to eight megabytes. After reconnecting, the client asks which parts arrived and sends only the missing ones.

scenes.title: Screen limit, step by step
bullets: Start: drop expired leases, count, add if under K
All of it in one atomic step per account
Player heartbeats every 60 s; lease TTL about 2 to 3 beats
Phone dies: no heartbeat, lease expires in minutes
Store down: fail open, log it, enforce when back

steps.say: On playback start, the concurrency service removes expired leases, counts the rest, and adds a new lease if the count is below the plan limit.
That has to be one atomic step per account, with a Lua script or a conditional write. Otherwise two devices starting together both grab the last slot.
While playing, the player heartbeats every sixty seconds, and the lease lives two or three heartbeats.
So when the phone dies, the heartbeats stop and the lease expires within a few minutes, freeing the slot.
And if the lease store is down, fail open and log it. Wrongly blocking a paying user is worse than a brief over-allowance.

head: Prompt
One-line answer skeleton
rows: 4 MB hashed chunks, delta sync, strong metadata
one owner per doc; OT or CRDT; op log
RRULE in the event's own time zone

steps.say: Seventh, files and collaboration. Dropbox: four megabyte chunks addressed by hash, so only changed chunks upload. Two offline edits make a conflicted copy.
Google Docs: route every editor of a document to one owner server. Operational transformation needs that central order. C-R-D-Ts merge without one, at the cost of extra metadata.
Google Calendar: store a recurring event once, as a rule, in the event's own time zone, so nine a-m every Monday stays at nine after daylight saving changes.
BitTorrent: peers fetch the rarest pieces first, upload to whoever gives them the best rate, and check every piece against its hash.
File downloader: range requests for resume, then verify and rename the dot-part file atomically.

scenes.title: Delta sync in numbers
bullets: A 1 GB file = 256 chunks of 4 MB
You edit one paragraph: one chunk's hash changes
Upload 4 MB instead of 1 GB: 256 times less
Same chunk hash elsewhere? Store it once: dedup

steps.say: A one gigabyte file at four megabytes a chunk is two hundred and fifty-six chunks.
You edit one paragraph. Only one chunk's content hash changes.
So the client uploads four megabytes instead of a gigabyte, two hundred and fifty-six times less data.
And if two users have a chunk with the same hash, it's stored once. That's dedup for free.

head: Prompt
One-line answer skeleton
rows: HELD where AVAILABLE, hold TTL, waiting room
waiting room, atomic counter, sold out at edge
atomic decrement plus unique per-user row

steps.say: Eighth, commerce and payments. Ticketmaster: a conditional update sets a seat to held only where it's still available, so one user wins each seat. Holds expire.
Hotel booking: an inventory row per hotel, room type and date, where reserved never exceeds total.
Payments: idempotency keys everywhere, a double-entry ledger, and reconciliation against bank files.
Flash sale: a waiting room, an atomic Redis counter, and sold out answered at the edge.
Coupons: an atomic conditional decrement for the usage limit, plus a unique key on campaign and user for one per person.
Stock exchange: a sequencer stamps every order, and a single-threaded matching engine per symbol is deterministic, so replicas replay the same input for failover.

scenes.title: Give away 6 million burgers in an hour
bullets: Pre-split stock: 600 shards × 10,000 vouchers
Atomic decrement per shard; empty? try another
6M ÷ 3,600 s ≈ 1,700 claims a second on average
First minutes: 10 to 100 times that, so queue it
One per person: unique key on the verified identity

steps.say: Give away exactly six million burger vouchers in one hour. Step one: pre-split the stock into six hundred shards of ten thousand vouchers, so no single counter is hot.
Step two: route each claim to a random shard and decrement atomically. If that shard's empty, try another.
Step three, the math: six million over three thousand six hundred seconds is about seventeen hundred claims a second on average.
But the first minutes see ten to a hundred times that, so a waiting room at the edge queues and smooths the burst.
Step five: one per person. A unique key on the verified identity, account plus phone or card, matters more than the counter.

head: Prompt
One-line answer skeleton
rows: DB apart, LB, replicas, cache, CDN, shard
pull or push, TSDB, watch label cardinality
leases with fencing tokens, idempotent jobs
agents, Kafka buffer, hot index, cold storage

steps.say: Ninth, infrastructure. Scale to millions: separate database, load balancer, stateless servers, replicas, cache, C-D-N, queues, then sharding.
Multiple regions: active-passive is simple; active-active needs conflict handling. Most replicate asynchronously and accept a small loss window.
S-three: a metadata service maps bucket and key to chunks, data nodes store them, and background repair keeps eleven nines of durability.
Metrics monitoring: pull or push collection into a time-series database. Watch cardinality: a label like user I-D creates a new series per user and blows up storage.
Job scheduler: workers take leases with fencing tokens, and jobs are idempotent, because exactly-once isn't realistic.
Logging: agents batch into Kafka, recent logs go to a search index, older ones to cheap object storage.
Here's the S-three probe, worked. Three full copies cost three times the storage. Eight data chunks plus four parity chunks cost twelve over eight, one and a half times.
And erasure coding survives any four lost chunks, versus any two lost copies.
The catch: repair reads eight chunks and burns more C-P-U.

scenes.title: Design X: developer and AI platforms

head: Prompt
One-line answer skeleton
rows: queue, sandboxed workers, no network, limits
token rate limits, SSE stream, batched GPUs
round location to grid cell, cache by cell

scenes.caption: Book: Module 22 · Developer and AI platforms

steps.say: Tenth, developer and A-I platforms. Online judge: a queue, and sandboxed workers with no network and hard limits.
Deployments: one immutable artifact, then canary, then waves, with automatic rollback.
ChatGPT: token rate limits, answers streamed over server-sent events, and continuous batching to stretch scarce G-P-Us.
A-B testing: hash the user I-D plus the experiment I-D into a bucket. It's deterministic, so assignment needs no database lookup.
Recommendations: a funnel. Generate candidates, rank them with a model, then re-rank for diversity and freshness.
Weather app: round the location to a grid cell, so requests share cache entries. Newer prompts add pub-sub, Twilio, code assistants and support bots.

scenes.title: The recommendation funnel in 100 ms
bullets: 10M items: scoring all of them per request is impossible
Candidates: several sources, a few hundred each
Rank about 1,000 with a model and feature store
Re-rank: diversity, freshness, drop already-seen
Ranker times out? Fall back to a cached list

steps.say: Let's work the funnel. Ten million items, a hundred milliseconds. Scoring ten million items per request is impossible.
Stage one: several candidate sources, like embedding neighbours and trending, each return a few hundred items.
Stage two: a ranking model scores about a thousand candidates with features from the feature store.
Stage three: re-rank with business rules, diversity and freshness, and drop items already consumed.
And if the ranker times out, return candidates in a simple order, or a cached list per user. Recap: narrow first, then rank.

scenes.title: Concepts: performance and scale
bullets: Latency = one request's time; throughput = per second
p99 shows your slowest users; averages hide them
Estimate: DAU × actions ÷ 100,000 s, × 2 to 3 for peak
Little's law: L = λ × W sizes pools and threads
Nines: 99.9% ≈ 8.8 h/year; series parts multiply
SLI measures, SLO targets, SLA contracts; error budget
scenes.caption: Book: Module 22 · Performance and scale

steps.say: Now Part B, the concept questions. First, performance and scale. Latency is how long one request takes, say forty milliseconds. Throughput is how many finish per second, say five thousand.
Why p ninety-nine, not the average? The average hides the slow few. p ninety-nine is what your unluckiest one percent feel.
Estimates: daily users times actions, over a hundred thousand seconds, times two or three for peak.
Little's law: requests in flight equals arrival rate times time inside. It tells you how many threads or connections you need.
Availability: ninety-nine point nine percent allows about eight point eight hours down a year. Parts in series multiply, so two of them give about ninety-nine point eight.
S-L-I is the measurement, S-L-O the internal target, S-L-A the contract with penalties. The error budget is one hundred percent minus the S-L-O.

scenes.title: Four numbers to say out loud

head: Question
Worked answer
rows: 99 at 10 ms + 1 at 5 s: mean ≈ 60 ms

steps.say: Here are the numbers. Ninety-nine requests at ten milliseconds and one at five seconds average about sixty milliseconds. That describes nobody.
A page calling a hundred backends hits at least one backend's p ninety-nine on about sixty-three percent of requests. Fan-out makes the tail the norm.
Little's law: a thousand requests a second at two hundred milliseconds each means about two hundred in flight.
And Q-P-S: ten million daily users times ten actions is a hundred million a day. Divide by a hundred thousand: about a thousand Q-P-S average, two to three thousand at peak.

scenes.title: Concepts: networking and APIs
bullets: Type a URL: DNS, TCP or QUIC, TLS, HTTP, render
TCP reliable and ordered; UDP fast; QUIC = UDP + streams
HTTP/2 multiplexes; HTTP/3 ends TCP head-of-line block
REST public; gRPC internal; GraphQL varied clients
Polling, long polling, SSE one-way, WebSocket two-way
Idempotent: GET, PUT, DELETE; cursor pagination
scenes.caption: Book: Module 22 · Networking and APIs

steps.say: Second, networking and A-P-Is. What happens when you type a U-R-L? D-N-S lookup, a T-C-P or QUIC connection, a T-L-S handshake, an H-T-T-P request through a load balancer, then rendering.
T-C-P is reliable and ordered. U-D-P has no guarantees, fine for calls and games. QUIC adds reliable, independent streams on U-D-P.
H-T-T-P two multiplexes streams on one connection, but one lost packet stalls them all. H-T-T-P three runs on QUIC, so streams recover independently.
REST for public A-P-Is, g-R-P-C for internal calls, GraphQL when clients need exactly their fields.
Real-time: server-sent events for one-way feeds, WebSockets for two-way chat and games.
GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent. POST isn't, so payments add an idempotency key. And prefer cursor pagination.

left.heading: Offset
bullets: LIMIT 20 OFFSET 10000
Scans and discards 10,000 rows
New posts shift items: repeats

right.heading: Cursor
bullets: WHERE (created_at, id) < cursor
Index seek: fast at any depth
Stable while data changes

steps.say: Imagine a feed, twenty items a page, and the user is on page five hundred. Offset pagination asks for limit twenty, offset ten thousand.
The database still scans and throws away ten thousand rows.
And while you scroll, new posts arrive, items shift, and you see repeats or miss some.
Cursor pagination hands back a token holding the last seen sort key, and asks for items older than it.
That's an index seek, fast at any depth.
And it's stable as data changes. The only cost is you can't jump to an arbitrary page.

scenes.title: Which of these is NOT idempotent?
bullets: GET /orders/42
PUT /orders/42
DELETE /orders/42
POST /payments

steps.say: Pause and think. Four requests. Which one is not idempotent, so repeating it after a timeout could do damage? Answer next.

scenes.title: Concepts: load balancing and caching
bullets: L4 routes by IP and port; L7 reads HTTP
Liveness = restart me; readiness = no traffic yet
Forward proxy for clients; reverse proxy for servers
Cache-aside, read-through, write-through, write-behind
LRU default; LFU keeps the popular; TTL as safety net
Write the DB, then delete the key; fix stampedes
scenes.caption: Book: Module 22 · Load balancing and caching

steps.say: It was POST: repeat it and you may charge twice. Now, load balancing and caching. An L-four balancer routes by I-P and port, very fast. An L-seven balancer reads H-T-T-P, so it can route by path, terminate T-L-S and retry.
Health checks: a failed liveness check means restart the process. A failed readiness check means stop sending traffic. Keep liveness cheap and local.
A forward proxy acts for clients; a reverse proxy acts for servers. An A-P-I gateway is a reverse proxy doing auth and rate limits once.
Cache-aside: check the cache, read the database on a miss, fill the cache. Write-through writes both. Write-behind writes the cache and flushes later, fast but risky.
L-R-U is the default eviction. L-F-U keeps popular items. A T-T-L is the safety net.
To stay consistent, update the database, then delete the key, rather than overwrite it.

scenes.title: A cache stampede, and four fixes
bullets: Hot product key expires; 5,000 requests miss at once
Fix 1: single flight: one request rebuilds the key
Fix 2: serve stale while one refresh runs
Fix 3: refresh early, before expiry
Fix 4: TTL jitter, e.g. 300 s ± 30 s

steps.say: Imagine a hot product page cached with a five minute T-T-L. It expires, and five thousand requests miss in the same second and all hit the database.
Fix one: single flight. One request takes a lock and rebuilds the key. The others wait for it.
Fix two: serve the stale value while that one refresh runs in the background.
Fix three: refresh hot keys probabilistically before they expire, so they never go cold.
Fix four: add jitter to T-T-Ls, say three hundred seconds plus or minus thirty, so keys don't all expire together.

scenes.title: Concepts: databases and storage
bullets: SQL for joins and ACID; NoSQL for simple access at scale
Families: key-value, document, wide-column, graph
Isolation: read committed, snapshot, serializable
B-tree reads fast; LSM tree writes fast
Optimistic vs pessimistic locking; MVCC snapshots
WAL for durability; pooling; avoid N+1 queries
scenes.caption: Book: Module 22 · Databases and storage

steps.say: Next, databases and storage. Choose S-Q-L for joins and transactions, like orders and payments. Choose No-S-Q-L when access is simple and scale is huge. Default to S-Q-L.
No-S-Q-L families: key-value for sessions, document for catalogs, wide-column for heavy time-ordered writes, graph for friends of friends.
Isolation levels: read committed stops dirty reads. Snapshot isolation gives a stable view but still allows write skew. Serializable prevents it all, at the cost of aborts.
A B-tree updates sorted pages in place, so reads and range scans are fast. An L-S-M tree buffers writes and merges sorted files later, so writes are fast.
Pessimistic locking locks before reading. Optimistic locking checks a version at write time. M-V-C-C keeps old row versions so readers never block writers.
The write-ahead log gives durability and feeds replication. Connection pools limit expensive connections.

scenes.title: Two fixes with real numbers
bullets: Optimistic: read row at version 7
UPDATE … WHERE id = 42 AND version = 7
Someone else wrote first: 0 rows updated, retry
N+1: 1 query for 100 posts + 100 author queries
Fix: one IN (…) batch: 101 queries become 2

steps.say: Two worked fixes. Optimistic locking: you read row forty-two at version seven.
You write with update, where i-d is forty-two and version is still seven, setting version to eight.
If someone wrote first, zero rows change, and you retry. No lock was held while the user was thinking.
Now the N plus one problem. An O-R-M loads a hundred posts with one query, then fetches each author separately: a hundred more.
Batch the authors into one query with an IN list. A hundred and one queries become two.

scenes.title: Concepts: replication and partitioning
bullets: Replication copies everything; sharding splits it
Leader-follower, multi-leader, leaderless
Sync: no loss, slower; async: fast, lag, small loss
Conflicts: last-write-wins, version vectors, CRDTs
Shard key: even spread, in most queries, not time
Consistent hashing with virtual nodes; reshard live
scenes.caption: Book: Module 22 · Replication and partitioning

steps.say: Replication and partitioning. Replication copies everything for reads and availability. Sharding splits data for write capacity. Big systems do both.
Leader-follower: one writer, no conflicts. Multi-leader: local writes per region, but conflicts. Leaderless, like Cassandra: quorums for reads and writes.
Synchronous replication loses nothing but every write waits. Asynchronous is fast, but replicas lag, so read your own recent writes from the leader.
Conflicts: last-write-wins is simple but drops data. Version vectors detect true concurrency. C-R-D-Ts always merge to the same result.
A good shard key spreads load and appears in most queries, like user I-D. Never a timestamp, which sends every new write to one shard. For a celebrity key, add a random suffix and merge on read.
To reshard live, use many more partitions than machines, copy a snapshot, stream changes, then switch.

scenes.title: Adding a fifth node
scenes.caption: hash(key) mod 4 → mod 5 versus consistent hashing

steps.say: Here's why consistent hashing matters. Go from four nodes to five. With hash of key mod N, a key stays put only if its value mod four equals its value mod five. That's about one in five, so about eighty percent of keys move.
On a hash ring, the new node takes just its slice, about one N-th, so about twenty percent move. And with virtual nodes, many points per server, that slice comes evenly from all four old nodes.

scenes.title: Concepts: consistency and consensus
bullets: CAP: in a partition pick CP or AP; PACELC: else L or C
Strong, read-your-writes, monotonic, causal, eventual
Quorum: R + W > N, e.g. N=3, W=2, R=2
2PC blocks on its coordinator; sagas compensate
Raft: majority elects a leader; 5 nodes survive 2
Locks need leases and fencing; clocks need logic
scenes.caption: Book: Module 22 · Consistency and consensus

steps.say: Consistency and consensus. CAP: during a partition, refuse requests to stay consistent, or answer with maybe-stale data. PACELC adds: else, latency versus consistency.
Consistency models run from linearizable, through read-your-writes and causal, to eventual. Pick the weakest each feature tolerates.
Quorums: write to W, read from R of N replicas. If R plus W is greater than N, every read overlaps the latest write.
Two-phase commit: prepare, then commit, atomic but blocking if the coordinator dies. A saga chains local transactions with compensations, like refund or release seat.
Raft: a follower that misses heartbeats becomes a candidate, and a majority vote makes it leader. Five nodes tolerate two failures.
Distributed locks need leases and fencing tokens. And since wall clocks drift, order events with Lamport, vector or hybrid logical clocks.

scenes.title: Fencing token in action
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  L["Lock service"] -->|"token 33"| A["Worker A"]
  A -->|"long GC pause"| X["Lease expires"]
  L -->|"token 34"| B["Worker B"]
  B -->|"write with 34"| S["Storage: max seen 34"]
  A -->|"late write with 33"| S
  S -->|"reject 33"| A
scenes.caption: Storage rejects any token older than the newest it has seen

steps.say: Imagine worker A holds a lock with token thirty-three, then freezes in a long garbage-collection pause. Its lease expires.
Worker B gets the lock with token thirty-four and writes. Storage now remembers thirty-four.
A wakes up and writes with thirty-three. Storage rejects it as stale. Without the token, both writes would land and corrupt the data.

scenes.title: Flight, hotel and car in 3 services: 2PC or saga?
bullets: Two-phase commit across all three
A saga with compensating actions

steps.say: Pause and think. One trip books a flight, a hotel and a car, each owned by a different service or even a different company. Two-phase commit or a saga? Answer next.

scenes.title: Concepts: messaging and streaming
bullets: Queue: one consumer per message; pub/sub: all of them
At-most-once, at-least-once; exactly-once effect
Kafka orders within a partition; key by entity
Batch vs stream; Lambda two paths, Kappa one
Event sourcing, CQRS, CDC, transactional outbox
Dead-letter queue for poison messages
scenes.caption: Book: Module 22 · Messaging and streaming

steps.say: A saga: local bookings, each with a compensation like cancel the flight, and no cross-company locks. Now, messaging. A queue gives each message to one consumer; pub-sub gives it to every subscriber. Kafka keeps a replayable log.
At-most-once can lose. At-least-once can duplicate, and it's the default. True exactly-once delivery isn't possible; you get exactly-once effect with idempotent processing or Kafka transactions.
Kafka orders only within a partition, so key messages by entity, like order I-D. Partitions cap a consumer group's parallelism, and offsets let consumers resume or replay.
Batch is simple but hours old; streams are fresh but handle late events. Lambda runs both paths; Kappa replays one stream.
Event sourcing stores every event as the truth. C-Q-R-S separates write and read models. C-D-C streams the database log, and the outbox avoids dual writes.
A dead-letter queue parks messages that keep failing, so one poison message can't block the queue.

scenes.title: An idempotent payment, step by step
bullets: Client sends POST /payments, key = a1b2 (a UUID)
Server charges, stores key + result in one transaction
Response is lost; client times out and retries
Server finds key a1b2: returns the stored result
Customer charged once, not twice

steps.say: An idempotent payment. The client sends a payment POST with an idempotency key, a fresh U-U-I-D, say a-one-b-two.
The server charges the card and stores the key with the result in the same transaction as the work.
The response is lost on the network. The client times out and retries with the same key.
The server finds a-one-b-two already stored and returns the saved result instead of charging again.
The customer is charged once. That's exactly-once effect built on at-least-once delivery.

scenes.title: Concepts: reliability and resilience
bullets: Remove SPOFs; active-passive vs active-active
Timeout from p99; retry few, idempotent, with jitter
Circuit breaker fails fast; bulkhead isolates pools
Backpressure, load shedding, graceful degradation
RPO = data you can lose; RTO = time you can be down
Rate limits: token bucket, leaky, windows; 429
scenes.caption: Book: Module 22 · Reliability and resilience

steps.say: Reliability and resilience. Remove single points of failure. Active-passive keeps an idle standby; active-active serves from all copies.
Every network call needs a timeout, set from the dependency's p ninety-nine. Retry only idempotent calls, a few times, with backoff and jitter, at one layer only.
A circuit breaker counts failures, opens to fail fast, then goes half-open to test. A bulkhead gives each dependency its own pool, so one slow one can't sink the service.
Backpressure tells producers to slow down. Load shedding rejects some requests so the rest succeed. Graceful degradation turns off extras, like recommendations, to keep the core path alive.
R-P-O is how much data you can lose, in time. R-T-O is how long you can be down.
Rate limiting: token bucket allows bursts, leaky bucket smooths, fixed windows allow double bursts at the edges.

scenes.title: Token bucket, worked
bullets: Bucket holds B = 10 tokens; refills R = 5 a second
A burst of 10 requests: all pass, bucket empty
Request 11 at once: 429 with Retry-After
After 1 second: 5 tokens back, 5 more pass
Long run: average 5/s, bursts up to 10

steps.say: A token bucket. It holds up to ten tokens and refills at five a second.
A client fires ten requests at once. Each takes a token, all pass, and the bucket is empty.
The eleventh request gets a four-twenty-nine with a Retry-After header.
One second later, five tokens are back, so five more requests pass.
Over time, the client averages five a second, but can burst up to ten. That's why the token bucket is the most common choice.

scenes.title: Concepts: security
bullets: AuthN = who you are; AuthZ = what you may do
Sessions revoke easily; JWTs scale, short-lived
OAuth 2.0 delegates; OIDC adds login; SSO
CORS, CSRF, XSS, SQL injection and their fixes
DDoS: absorb at the edge; WAF blocks bad patterns
Slow salted hashes, KMS, vault; least privilege
scenes.caption: Book: Module 22 · Security

steps.say: Security. Authentication checks who you are. Authorization decides what you may do, and it always comes second.
Sessions are easy to revoke but need a lookup. A J-W-T verifies without a lookup but is hard to revoke, so keep it short-lived.
O-Auth two delegates access; OpenID Connect adds login; single sign-on reuses it across apps.

CORS relaxes a browser rule; it doesn't protect your server. CSRF is fixed with SameSite cookies and tokens. XSS with output escaping and a content security policy. S-Q-L injection with parameterized queries.
D-DoS: let C-D-Ns and anycast absorb floods, and rate limit application floods. A web application firewall blocks known attack patterns.
Hash passwords with a slow, salted function like Argon-two or bcrypt. Keep keys in a K-M-S and secrets in a vault. Least privilege and zero trust shrink the blast radius.

scenes.title: Log in with OpenID Connect
bullets: App redirects you to the identity provider, with PKCE
You log in and consent; the app gets a one-time code
App swaps the code for tokens on the back channel
ID token: who you are; access token: 15 min to call APIs
Refresh token gets new access tokens; rotate it

steps.say: A login with OpenID Connect. Step one: the app redirects you to the identity provider, using PKCE to prove it's the same app at the end.
Step two: you log in and consent, and the provider sends the app a one-time code.
Step three: the app exchanges that code for tokens, server to server, never in the browser's address bar.
Step four: the I-D token says who you are. The access token, valid for maybe fifteen minutes, lets the app call A-P-Is.
Step five: a refresh token gets new access tokens. Rotate it on every use, so a stolen one is detected when it's reused.

scenes.title: Concepts: operations
bullets: Start with a modular monolith; split when it hurts
Discovery, sidecars, service mesh with mTLS
Blue-green switches; canary widens; flags release
Metrics, logs, traces, tied by one trace ID
Alert on SLO burn rate, not CPU; golden signals
Containers and Kubernetes; autoscale with a cap
scenes.caption: Book: Module 22 · Operations

steps.say: Operations. Monolith or microservices? Start with a modular monolith, and split when team size or scaling needs justify it.
A service mesh is sidecar proxies plus a control plane, giving every call m-T-L-S, retries and metrics.
Blue-green runs two environments and switches all traffic at once. A canary sends one percent, then ten, and widens or rolls back. Feature flags separate deploying code from releasing a feature.
Observability: metrics for dashboards and alerts, structured logs for detail, traces for one request's path, all joined by a trace I-D.
Alert on symptoms users feel, measured against S-L-Os, with burn-rate alerts. Dashboards follow the four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors and saturation.
Kubernetes schedules and restarts containers. Autoscaling needs cooldowns and a maximum.

scenes.title: Rename a column with zero downtime
bullets: Expand: add new column; old code still works
Deploy code that writes both old and new
Backfill old rows in small batches
Switch reads to new; check results match
Contract: stop writing old, then drop it

steps.say: Rename a column with zero downtime, using expand and contract. Step one, expand: add the new column.
Step two: deploy code that writes to both columns.
Step three: backfill existing rows in small batches, so you don't lock the table.
Step four: switch reads to the new column and check the results match.
Step five, contract: stop writing the old column, then drop it. Every step can roll back on its own.

scenes.title: Concepts: algorithms and data structures
bullets: Bloom filter, HyperLogLog, count-min sketch
Merkle trees find differences; anti-entropy repairs
Geohash prefixes plus 8 neighbours; quadtree adapts
IDs: auto-increment, UUIDv4, UUIDv7, Snowflake
Top K: heap; inverted index with BM25 ranking
Skip list in Redis sorted sets; HNSW vector search
scenes.caption: Book: Module 22 · Algorithms and data structures

steps.say: Last of Part B, algorithms and data structures. These trade a little accuracy for big memory savings. A Bloom filter says definitely not, or probably yes. HyperLogLog counts distinct items. A count-min sketch estimates frequency and never undercounts.
A Merkle tree is a tree of hashes. Replicas compare roots and walk down only branches that differ.
Geohash: a shared prefix means nearby, so search the cell and its eight neighbours. A quadtree splits busy squares into four, adapting to density.
I-Ds: UUID version four is random and scatters index inserts; version seven and Snowflake are time-ordered.
Top K: a hash map and a min-heap of size K. An inverted index maps each term to its documents, ranked by T-F-I-D-F or B-M-twenty-five.
Redis sorted sets use a skip list plus a hash table, perfect for leaderboards. Vector search uses approximate nearest neighbour indexes like H-N-S-W, trading a little recall for speed.

scenes.title: A crawler's Bloom filter
bullets: Billions of URLs: a full set won't fit in memory
New URL: check the Bloom filter
'Definitely not seen': crawl it, add it
'Probably seen': skip; rare false positives OK
Never a false negative: no page fetched twice by it

steps.say: A crawler has seen billions of U-R-Ls. A full set won't fit in memory.
So every new U-R-L is checked against a Bloom filter, a bit array with a few hash functions.
If it says definitely not seen, crawl it and add it.
If it says probably seen, skip it. Missing the odd page is an acceptable price.
It never gives a false negative, so a seen U-R-L is never crawled twice.

scenes.title: Top 60 fundamentals questions
bullets: Q1 to Q13: foundations and performance
Q14 to Q28: networking and communication
Q29 to Q40: data storage
Q41 to Q54: caching, async and consistency
Q55 to Q60: architecture, reliability, security
Goal: each answer in your own words, with a number
scenes.caption: Book: Module 0 · Top 60 interview questions

steps.say: Now the Top sixty from Module zero, the questions asked most in phone screens. One to thirteen are foundations, like Little's law and the nines.
Fourteen to twenty-eight: networking, from D-N-S to load balancers and pagination.
Twenty-nine to forty: data storage, from A-C-I-D to shard keys.
Forty-one to fifty-four: caching, queues, idempotency, CAP, quorums and sagas.
Fifty-five to sixty: architecture, reliability and security. Circuit breakers, jitter, token buckets, auth, R-P-O and R-T-O.
The test: if you can answer all sixty in your own words, each with a number or an example, you have the fundamentals an interviewer expects.

head: Question
Answer with a number
rows: read own writes from the primary
uneven load; use a shared session store

steps.say: Rapid fire. What does four nines mean? Ninety-nine point nine nine percent, about fifty-two and a half minutes down a year.
Error budget at three nines? Point one percent of requests, about forty-three minutes a month.
Replication lag? A user may not see their own comment. Read their recent writes from the primary.
Sticky sessions? They work, but load is uneven and sessions die with the server. Prefer a shared session store.
Why jitter? Backoff of one, two, four, eight seconds gives room, but clients that failed together retry together. Randomness spreads them.
R-P-O of five minutes? Backups or replication must never fall more than five minutes behind.

head: Term
One line, with an example
rows: one IP, many sites; nearest one answers
slow consumer tells producers to slow
how much a failure can hit; cells limit it
stream DB changes from its log (Debezium)
copy author name into posts: no join

steps.say: Finally, the A to Z glossary from Module zero. Anycast: many servers announce one I-P, and the network routes each user to the nearest. C-D-Ns use it.
Backpressure: a slow consumer tells producers to slow down, instead of letting a queue grow until memory runs out.
Blast radius: how much of the system one failure can hit. Cell-based architecture caps it.
Change data capture: streaming a database's changes from its own log, for example with Debezium, to keep search and caches in sync.
Denormalization: copying data, like the author's name into every post, so reads skip a join.
Error budget: one minus the S-L-O. At three nines, that's point one percent of requests.

head: Term
One line, with an example
rows: rising number; storage drops stale holders
celebrity profile overloads one cache node
client UUID so retries act once
a lock that expires unless renewed
no partition? still latency vs consistency
N=3, W=2, R=2 overlap on the latest write

steps.say: F to Q. Fencing token: a number that rises with every lock grant, so storage rejects a paused old holder.
Hot key: one entry, like a celebrity profile, so popular it maxes out the node that holds it.
Idempotency key: a client-supplied I-D so a retried request acts only once.
Lease: a lock or role that expires unless renewed, so a crashed holder can't block forever.
PACELC: even without a partition, you still trade latency against consistency.
Quorum: the minimum replicas that must take part. Three, two, two means every read overlaps the latest write.

head: Term
One line, with an example
rows: you always see your own new comment
two leaders after a partition; majority fixes
p99 and p999: the slowest requests
two on-call doctors both sign off
verify every call, even inside the network

steps.say: R to Z. Read-your-writes: you always see your own recent update, like the comment you just posted.
Saga: a chain of local transactions with compensations, like a refund, instead of one distributed lock.
Split brain: a partition leaves two nodes both acting as leader. A majority quorum and fencing prevent it.
Tail latency: the slowest requests, p ninety-nine and p nine-nine-nine. Fan-out makes them common.
Write skew: two transactions each read that two doctors are on call, each lets one go home, and together they leave nobody. Only serializable isolation stops it.
Zero trust: never trust a call just because it's inside the network. Authenticate every request, for example with mutual T-L-S.
